Release: Document version: Document number: Printed in Sweden 9903 493-0192-11 3-2 Foreword Since the first edition of the COMLI system description was published, significant changes have taken place both on ABB Automation’s control systems and the COMLI protocol. New systems have been launched and old systems have become obsolete. This has produced new demands on COMLI resulting in new messages emerging and old messages disap- pearing. In this new version, the chapters related to individual control systems have been omitted to facilitate future updating. Instead, the reader is referred to the COMLI description for the relevant system. Major sec- tions of the description have also been restructured. COMLI is a conventional communication link using serial, asynchronous data transmission in half duplex mode, i.e. one direction at a time, and according to the master/slave principle. This document provides detailed information on COMLI for personnel requir- ing a thorough understanding of the system in order to implement COMLI in a particular application or locate faults on a system. The description assumes a knowledge of ABB Automation’s control systems and the terminology used in the control system descriptions.

COMLI is the most common data communication system used with the ABB Automation family of control systems. Latest generation installations provid- ing operator presentation as well as PLC facilities may use new data transmis- sion systems such as MMS. When COMLI is also used in these new systems, implementation is slightly different to when COMLI is used for data commu- nication between SattCon systems only. Throughout this description it is assumed that only SattCon systems are used. Definitions Master and Slave The terms master and slave are used frequently throughout this handbook. Master in a communications context means the controlling station which always initiates the message transmission sequence. Slave means a reply sta- tion which cannot start a communication sequence but simply responds to calls from the Master station. This is indicated by the suffix H after the hexadecimal characters. The data in the last byte of the message is coded in hexadecimal format, other bytes are coded in ASCII-hexadecimal format. I/O-bit ABB Automation’s control systems include a memory area called I/O RAM containing the I/O rack’s digital input and output signal statuses. In addition to I/O RAM, storage for memory cells, timer indications, limiter modules etc. is also included. An advantage with I/O RAM is that unused channels on the input and output cards can be used as working memory cells for temporary storage of intermediate results. Throughout the remainder of this description the term I/O bit refers to a location in this I/O RAM. 2 COMLI Letter codes The following letters are used to identify the various types of address: P = an address of 16 contiguous I/O-bits in I/O-RAM. R = 16-bit register address. 1.2 COMLI - principle of operation ABB Automation’s systems communicate with each other and with other com- puters using COMLI (COMmunication LInk). COMLI is one of ABB Auto- mation’s communication networks using serial, asynchronous data transmission in half duplex mode (one direction at a time) and in accordance with the Master/Slave principle (the Slave does not reply if there is an error in the message received). Master and Slave can be linked together in different ways to achieve the desired function, i.e. Point-to-Point, Multipoint (Multidrop) or radial configu- ration (see the section on Network configuration). Up to 32 Slave systems can be connected to a Master system in a multipoint configuration. Master and Slave are linked via the serial channels on the different systems which are to communicate with each other. Master and Slave need not use the same physi- cal channel numbers in both the systems. They must however have the same character format, transmission speed etc. Communication is controlled by the PLC programs in the different contro

e same physi- cal channel numbers in both the systems. They must however have the same character format, transmission speed etc. Communication is controlled by the PLC programs in the different control sys- tems. By activating a predetermined memory cell, the PLC program in the control system acting as Master transmits a message. When the Slave receives the message, it responds either by sending the requested information or by acknowledging the information received. The memory cell is reset when the Master receives the information or an acknowledgement from the Slave. The information in ABB Automation's control systems is stored in the differ- ent memory modules. About 50 different message types are defined for the various types of information to be transferred. When the master starts a communication sequence, a communication area determines the type of data to be transferred. The data is transmitted and received via a serial channel defined using a channel definition area. Network configurations There are two network configurations for a COMLI serial communication net- work: • Multipoint communication • Point to point communication COMLI 3 Multipoint communication Several Slave sy

figurations There are two network configurations for a COMLI serial communication net- work: • Multipoint communication • Point to point communication COMLI 3 Multipoint communication Several Slave systems are connected to a master in multipoint communication. Communication takes place between Master and one Slave at a time. Direct communication between Slave systems is not possible. A particular message from the Master is applied to all Slaves but only the slave whose unique iden- tity corresponds to the identity contained in the message accepts the data. The number of Slaves which can be connected to each Master is limited by the communication interface. The RS485 interface must be used in multipoint communication. The Master transmit line is connected to all Slave receive lines and all Slave transmit lines are commoned and connected to the Master receive line. RS485 permits 32 Slave systems to be connected to a Master. The COMLI communications software can handle a maximum of 247 Slaves. Example of multipoint communication Point to point - communication In point to point communication, only one Slave system is connected to the Master via one communication interface. Several Slav

aves. Example of multipoint communication Point to point - communication In point to point communication, only one Slave system is connected to the Master via one communication interface. Several Slaves can be connected to the Master but this must take place via different communication interfaces. This form of point to point configuration is called a radial (star) network and can provide a higher capacity than multipoint communication. The electrical interface can be either RS232/V24 or RS485. A current loop can also be used in certain special cases. This is stated in the relevant system description. Example of point-to-point communication Master The Master always initiates the message transmission sequence, whether transmitting data to a slave or requesting data from a slave. The main functions of the Master are: • To transmit data to the Slaves and receive the data transmitted by the Slaves. • To process the messages received from the Slave. • To repeat a message transmission if errors occur. Since the Slave never replies with an “error message”, the Master always knows how many characters it should receive in a message. If the Master requests a certain quantity of data, the Slave replies with the stated number of bytes or not at all. Up to 10 retransmissions can be attempted if any errors are detected (the actual number permitted is system dependent). This is followed by automatic error message printouts in earlier SattCon systems. About .NET installations Top About .NET installations The .NET framework, in addition to making across the Web inter-operability simpler and easier also provides the a number of advantages when it comes to deploying and maintaining applications when compared to conventional software in the past. Advantages of .NET installations over conventional software installations: In the past one of the greatest headache with installing (deploying) applications, were shared DLLs (dynamic-link libraries), which has been termed "DLL Hell" for the following reasons: Firstly, these files needed to be dispersed across hard disk in common folders, such as System32. This both complicated the process of backing up and removing these applications and caused the hard drive to become cluttered with these files. Secondly, these files could easily be overwritten by newer versions that were not backward compatible with the version already on the computer. Which could cause one or more of the existing applications to either work incorrectly or stop working completely. .NET applications, however, prevent potential conflicts between applications by isolating their assemblies formerly known as a dynamic linked

ns to either work incorrectly or stop working completely. .NET applications, however, prevent potential conflicts between applications by isolating their assemblies formerly known as a dynamic linked libraries (.DLL files), which is externally compiled and contains a collection of properties or methods that can be implemented within a script. in their individual installation folders. For this reason, multiple versions of an assembly can be installed and run simultaneously on the same computer. Furthermore .NET applications record the version information of its component assemblies and verify these versions before it is run. Any version differences detected prevent the application from running and display an appropriate warning instead. Therefore .NET applications always load the components with which they were built and tested. In the past applications were forced to use the registry to store their user-configurable settings and any other application-specific information, which in many cases complicated the process of replicating and backing up these applications effectively. .NET applications are no longer tied to using the registry to save its user-customizable settings. Instead these settings are saved in .CONFIG files (a type of .INI file), which reside within the application’s installation folder and can be opened and edited in any text editor. In short by making .NET applications entirely self-contained the major hiccups that previously complicating the process of installing, copying, backing up and removing conventional software, have been removed. This means that the installation folder of a .NET application now contains: All of its dependent assemblies formerly known as a dynamic linked libraries (.DLL files), which is externally compiled and contains a collection of properties or methods that can be implemented within a script. , with each assembly having the specific version that this application was built and tested with. All the user-customizable settings for the application, contained within its .CONFIG file This .NET file is similar to an .INI file, in a single .CONFIG file is used per application to contain its user-configurable settings. This text file is located in the installation folder and has the same name as its application. . Although this does mean that it is no longer essential to install a .NET application, an installation is still preferred, since it does still makes it easier to manage the copied files and to perform any further configuration, such as the setting up of services etc. Note: If you do not install the product, then you will need to run the .NET framework’s InitExe application to install the required .NET services, yourself. -->

About Adroit Backup Utility Top About Adroit Backup Utility How to Use this Adroit Backup Utility The Adroit Backup Utility makes it possible to create a complete backup of your Adroit installation. This should be used to protect your Adroit installation from corruption or possible accidental deletion and also provides an easy way for transferring an Adroit project or system to another computer. This consists of the following 4 sections, which can be enabled or disabled according to your needs: Adroit installation files : backs up the files required by the Adroit application. Adroit data files : backs up the files required by your Adroit projects, where multiple file locations can be specified. Event Logs : ONLY exports the application; security and system event logs files. These event log files CANNOT be restored but can be viewed. Adroit registry : backs up both the global Adroit registry settings and the Adroit registry settings specific to the current user. Once the back up has been appropriately configured, click the Backup now button to execute the back up. The Backup path , allows you to specify where these Adroit backups are to be stored . The Overwrite option determines if

n appropriately configured, click the Backup now button to execute the back up. The Backup path , allows you to specify where these Adroit backups are to be stored . The Overwrite option determines if previous backups are preserved or overwritten , affecting the structure of the saved backup directory . The Adroit Backup Utility makes use of profiles to store different backup configuration settings for later reuse and as these profiles can be executed from the command-line , Adroit backups are also able to be scheduled or run from a batch file. The Set defaults button can be used to save the configured backup settings as the Default profile settings, this is recommended if the current settings are to be frequently used. On exit the currently configured settings are saved to the currently selected profile . -->

About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) Top About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) The Agent Server is a collection or container of the supported agent types and stores and manages the instances of their created agents, by providing consistent mechanisms for creating and destroying agents and accessing the information contained within them. Each agent type is a Windows Dynamic Link Library (.DLL) file in the Adroit system folder, which is loaded when the Agent Server starts up, making its functionality available for use. The Adroit database (.WGP) file or load file stores almost all of the data and configuration of the Agent Server. This includes every agent that has been added to the current project of this Agent Server, with the exception of the agents that are automatically created or dynamic agents like Proxy and Scan agents. Note: For this reason it essential that this Adroit database (.WGP) file is frequently backed up. For details, see Backing Up Adroit Database (.WGP) Files . About Adroit Projects Top About Adroit Projects A project in Adroit , is the default mechanism for allowing multiple distributed Agent Servers to seamlessly share their agents and the data that they contain. In other words, if Agent Server A and Agent Server B have the SAME project name (and are in the same network domain), then Agent Server A is able to refer to agents within Agent Server B and vice verse. For further details of how Adroit projects work and their limitations and the other mechanisms that are provided to overcome these limitations, see Agent Server Connection Methods . Note: Proxy agents are automatically created when an Agent Server accesses an agent that exists in a remote Agent Server. This provides client applications with a transparent mechanism for accessing agents, so that a distributed agent database acts as a standalone database. In other words, even though a Classic UI connects to a single Agent Server, one or its mimics or pictures can display agents that exist on a remote Agent Server. All Agent Servers need to specify a project name whether they are standalone (a single Agent Server on one computer) or distributed (requiring more than one Agent Server)

ist on a remote Agent Server. All Agent Servers need to specify a project name whether they are standalone (a single Agent Server on one computer) or distributed (requiring more than one Agent Server). While it is essential that each Agent Server has a unique name, project names should only be the same for those Agent Server that are required to communicate to one another. Configure the required Project and Agent Server name in the Agent Server Configuration page of the Adroit Configuration utility. A number of other configuration requirements must be met before a distributed project can be created. For details, see Requirements for Distributed Agent Servers. For details, see Best Practices . For details, see About Backup Procedures . -->

About Agent Data (Slots) Top About Agent Data (Slots) Each agent (instance of an agent type) maintains its own unique set of data and is referred to by its own unique agent name. For details, see About Agents or Naming Agents . Most agents are designed to contain multiple items of data, which are referred to as agent attributes. Most of these attributes are accessible to clients of the Agent Server as slots of the agent. Slots can therefore be defined as externally accessible attributes of an agent. For details, see Accessing Agent Slots . For instance, the Analog agent slot has a hiHi slot that allows a value to be assigned that represents the high-high alarm limit for an analog signal. There are clearly different types of data that need to be stored in an agent. For example, the name, is an ASCII string, whereas the hiHi limit, referred to above, is a floating point Real number value, and the state of a Digital is a Boolean TRUE/FALSE indication. This implies the concept of slot type , as well as agent type. For details, see Slot Types . An Adroit configuration is therefore made of many different agents, each of which is a unique instance of one of the supported agent types. Each

, as well as agent type. For details, see Slot Types . An Adroit configuration is therefore made of many different agents, each of which is a unique instance of one of the supported agent types. Each agent, in turn, contains externally accessible data attributes, or slots, whose type corresponds to one of the supported slot types. For details of the available slots for each agent type, see Agent Type Slot Reference . An agent's "state", at any instant in time, is defined as the collective values of all its data. About Agent Servers Top About Agent Servers The Agent Server is the storage facility for all real time and historical data. The real time data resides within intelligent objects, known as agents, which exchange messages with other agents or picture objects either from their local host computer or from remote computer nodes elsewhere on the network. Historical data is written to disk where it is available for rapid retrieval and on-line analysis. Note: Redundancy can be provided by configuring the Agent Server as a cluster server, which is a set of two Agent Servers running a replicated database. For details, see About Active Clustering and Important Points to consider when Clustering Agent Servers . Agents are described as intelligent because they store live data as well as providing methods of manipulating that data. Agents can be both clients and servers at the same time, by operating on, and being operated upon, by other agents. For details, see About Agents . The interaction of the agents with each other as well as with the Classic User Interface and its picture objects, provides a powerful and dynamic monitoring and control capability which reflects the status of your process

agents with each other as well as with the Classic User Interface and its picture objects, provides a powerful and dynamic monitoring and control capability which reflects the status of your process in real-time. For further details, see What you can do in Adroit . Agents are classified by function into a number of agent types, which can be used to implement a wide variety of system related, as well as application-specific tasks. For details, see About Agent Types . Note: An instance of an agent type is usually referred to as an agent. The Agent Server is therefore a collection or container of the supported agent types and stores and manages the instances of their created agents, in an agent database (.WGP) file. For further details regarding the storage of agents, see About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) . Note: The Agent Server is the only component in Adroit that needs to be licensed. About Agent Types Top About Agent Types Adroit configurations are composed of intelligent, cooperating objects known as agents . For details, see About Agents . These agents are differentiated into different types to provide specific information storage and manipulation mechanisms, with their intended function determining their complexity. By default, these agent types are further separated into the following categories to better facilitate the selection of the required agent when designing your system, as follows: Basic : these agent types form the basic building blocks of a system and are used for gathering, handling and processing data to and from the physical external world. Analog, Counter, Date, Digital, Expression, Marshal, MultiState, String, StringList, Timer Advanced : these agent types provide powerful SCADA and integration functionality that allow the Basic agents to be alarmed and logged to databases and provides various means of reporting and/or controlling their values. MaxDemand, OEE, PID IT : these agent types facilitate the integration and management of SCADA and IT Audit, DumpConfig, ICMP, Perfmon, SNMPMgr System : these agent types are used internally to perform certain SCADA and other specific functions. About Agents Top About Agents The Agent Server is the storage facility for all agents. For details, see About Agent Servers . Agents are called agents because, instead of only containing data, like simple database records, they also usually contain the ability to operate or act on their own data, driving its values and to read and write to other objects, and so influence them. This concept is very much in line with object-oriented thinking, and is primarily why we refer to Adroit as being "object-oriented". Note: When referring to a data value within an agent this is often referred to as a tag. For details, see Agents, Slots, Tags and their relation to Values . Agents are classified by function into a number of agent types, which can be used to implement a wide variety of system related, as well as application-specific tasks. For details, see About Agent Types . For example, the Analog agent type is used to handle the signal conditioning and alarm checking requirements of a process variable, and the DataLog agent type is responsible for creating, maintaining, and accessing historical data logs. An agent is therefore, more correctly, an instance of an agent type, for example an inst

iable, and the DataLog agent type is responsible for creating, maintaining, and accessing historical data logs. An agent is therefore, more correctly, an instance of an agent type, for example an instance of the Analog agent type could be the TANKLEVEL Analog agent (assuming that this agent has been created by a user). Each of these agent types have well defined rules for interfacing with other agents ensuring that an extremely robust and versatile environment has been created to handle any real world situation. For this reason each Adroit agent can be dynamically configured to benefit from specific functions provided by other agent types, such as scanning ( Communicating Values ), alarming ( Alarming Values ) and logging ( Logging values ). The interaction of these agents with each other as well as with the Classic User Interface and its picture objects, provides a powerful and dynamic monitoring and control capability which reflects the status of your process in real-time. For each agent type, there may be zero, one or many agent instances. Each time you add an agent, you are creating a new agent instance, however, agent instances are simply referred to as agents. Every agent, wi

gent type, there may be zero, one or many agent instances. Each time you add an agent, you are creating a new agent instance, however, agent instances are simply referred to as agents. Every agent, with the exception of the agents that are automatically created or dynamic agents like Proxy and Scan agents, are stored in an Adroit database (.WGP) file. For details, see About Adroit Database Files (Agent Storage) . About Alarm Acknowledgement Top About Alarm Acknowledgement Acknowledgment is typically recommended for alarms or incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). that require some sort of reaction or attention from the operator. In other words, an alarm should be any event that an operator must understand, acknowledge and respond to – and not simply acknowledge and ignore. Therefore you should carefully consider, which incidents require acknowledgement and which do not. Adroit provides the following methods of acknowledging alarms: Global acknowledgement: This should be used when using a standalone Adroit installation or for those alarms that only one operator needs to be made aware of. By globally acknowledging an alarm from any computer in the network, this incident will be removed from ALL the lists in the system (provided, of course, that the alarm is no longer active). Local acknowledgement: This should be used when you have alarms that more that one operator needs to be aware of. Click for mor

in the system (provided, of course, that the alarm is no longer active). Local acknowledgement: This should be used when you have alarms that more that one operator needs to be aware of. Click for more details: In other words you have a distributed Adroit installation, with operators viewing the process from remote user interfaces. Local acknowledge refers to the action of acknowledging an alarm in an alarm list of an AlarmList agent. This removes the alarm from this alarm list, provided the alarm is no longer active. If the alarm is routed to other alarm lists (usually on other computers), locally acknowledging the alarm one alarm list will not clear the alarm from these other alarm lists. This method therefore requires that each operator locally (remotely) acknowledges the alarm, to remove it from their alarm list (once it is no longer active the monitored condition of this incident (alarm/event) is still in effect and has not yet returned to its normal operating state. ). Note1: In the case of local alarm acknowledgement, you need to use the AlarmList agent to contain these incidents and NOT the Alarm agent. For further details of using AlarmLists and displaying alarms, see Disp

the case of local alarm acknowledgement, you need to use the AlarmList agent to contain these incidents and NOT the Alarm agent. For further details of using AlarmLists and displaying alarms, see Displaying Alarms . Note2: Once an incident has been locally (remotely) acknowledged from a remote UI, the color of this alarm changes (to blue by default) so that the other operators can see that this has occurred. However, each operator that views this alarm still needs to locally acknowledge it before it is removed from the list. Only when this alarm is globally acknowledged is it removed from the global alarm list of the Alarm agent. For more details about enabling or disabling the acknowledgement of incidents, see Configuring Incident Acknowledgement . For details about acknowledging alarms using the Alarm List Viewer window, see Acknowledging Alarms. Note: To define how the alarming subsystem treats current alarms if an agent’s statusalarmInhibit slot is set to one and the agent is currently in alarm and/or unacknowledged, add and configure the SmartInhibit registry value. If you route incidents to an AlarmManagement agent, then instead of operators simply acknowledging an incident,

ntly in alarm and/or unacknowledged, add and configure the SmartInhibit registry value. If you route incidents to an AlarmManagement agent, then instead of operators simply acknowledging an incident, by pressing a button, you can have them: specify the reason and sub-reason that caused this incident and/or specify additional notes relating to this incident. These measures will improve your incident reviews. You can also have your operators launch a HTML document relating specifically to each incident to help them both UNDERSTAND and RESPOND appropriately to this incident. For details of how to use the AlarmManagement agent, see Quick Start to Configure and Record Incidents (Alarms/Events) . For details about hiding or showing the local and/or global acknowledgement buttons of the Alarm List Viewer window, see Securing Acknowledge Buttons in Alarm Windows. -->

About Alarm Management Top About Alarm Management Alarm management is concerned with improving the QUALITY of the information within the alarming configuration. This information should be used to reduce the QUANTITY of nuisance alarms (red herrings) so that only the most important and relevant alarms are displayed for your process. In other words, alarm management can counteract inefficient alarming. Up to now SCADA installations have used numerous alarms, each of which usually have very little awareness of the other alarms in the system. So generally each incident generates a flood of alarms, which operators simply ignore because there are too many to deal with. According to the EEMUA 191 guidelines a document created by the Engineering Equipment & Materials Users' Association ( EEMUA) of alarm management guidelines, developed by the users of alarm systems, and is the globally accepted and leading guide to good practice for alarm management. : An alarm is an incident that an operator must understand, acknowledge and respond to – not simply acknowledge and ignore. For further details, see Effective Alarm Characteristics . No process should have more than 6 such alarm occurrences an

must understand, acknowledge and respond to – not simply acknowledge and ignore. For further details, see Effective Alarm Characteristics . No process should have more than 6 such alarm occurrences an hour during normal operations. Under abnormal process conditions no more than 10 alarms per minute should occur. Your SCADA installation requires an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. In this case fewer alarms are more effective as the human mind can only focus on a few things at a time. ondition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). . Note: By repeating this process regularly, you will be able to ensure that only relevant alarms are generated thereby improving your alarming system. Adroit has improved the legacy alarming system, to allow you to assign a priority PER ALARM (previously priorities could only be assigned PER AGENT), which allows your operators to filter out lower priority alarms, if required. About Alarm Management Top The Why and How of Alarm Management in Adroit Why is alarm management needed? In the past alarms were hardwired into the panels, which limited their number; now that alarms are software-driven, means that you can have an unlimited number of alarms. In an effort to keep the operators sufficiently informed, SCADA installations typically use lots of alarms, each of which usually have very little awareness of the other alarms in the system. This means that each incident can generate a flood of alarms, which causes operators to become overloaded and confused and as a result they may even start ignoring alarms! Therefore LESS alarms are MORE effective. Alarm management is concerned with improving the QUALITY of the information within the alarming configuration. This information should be used to reduce the QUANTITY of nuisance alarms (red herrings) so that only the most important and relevant alarms are displayed for your process. In other words alarm management counteracts inefficient alarming by allowing you to create an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. The following procedure describes the recommen

unteracts inefficient alarming by allowing you to create an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. The following procedure describes the recommended method of using the AlarmManagement agent to configure and record your active incidents so that you can analyse this information to improve your alarming configuration. What is an incident? In Adroit, Alarm agents can monitor other agents for preset conditions or states. So that when a monitored condition occurs in an agent its Alarm agent uses predefined reporting methods to alert the necessary people and/or applications. That is why Alarming in Adroit primarily involves the configuration of the following two things: The preset conditions or states of each agent that you need to alarm, known as alarm types, which each constitute a separate alarm or event. The alarm routes that specify which alarm destinations (reporting mechanisms) you need to use to communicate the generated alarms and events to the necessary personnel and/or applications. In Adroit an incident occurs when an agent enters a condition defined by an alarm type that is being monitored by an Alarm agent. However, an

nd events to the necessary personnel and/or applications. In Adroit an incident occurs when an agent enters a condition defined by an alarm type that is being monitored by an Alarm agent. However, an incident is ONLY an alarm, if it needs to be responded to; otherwise it is an event. -->

About Alarm Management Top The Why and How of Alarm Management in Adroit Why is alarm management needed? In the past alarms were hardwired into the panels, which limited their number; now that alarms are software-driven, means that you can have an unlimited number of alarms. In an effort to keep the operators sufficiently informed, SCADA installations typically use lots of alarms, each of which usually have very little awareness of the other alarms in the system. This means that each incident can generate a flood of alarms, which causes operators to become overloaded and confused and as a result they may even start ignoring alarms! Therefore LESS alarms are MORE effective. Alarm management is concerned with improving the QUALITY of the information within the alarming configuration. This information should be used to reduce the QUANTITY of nuisance alarms (red herrings) so that only the most important and relevant alarms are displayed for your process. In other words alarm management counteracts inefficient alarming by allowing you to create an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. The following procedure describes the recommen

unteracts inefficient alarming by allowing you to create an alarming system that alerts the operator to the most relevant alarm for the current incident. The following procedure describes the recommended method of using the AlarmManagement agent to configure and record your active incidents so that you can analyse this information to improve your alarming configuration. What is an incident? In Adroit, Alarm agents can monitor other agents for preset conditions or states. So that when a monitored condition occurs in an agent its Alarm agent uses predefined reporting methods to alert the necessary people and/or applications. That is why Alarming in Adroit primarily involves the configuration of the following two things: The preset conditions or states of each agent that you need to alarm, known as alarm types, which each constitute a separate alarm or event. The alarm routes that specify which alarm destinations (reporting mechanisms) you need to use to communicate the generated alarms and events to the necessary personnel and/or applications. In Adroit an incident occurs when an agent enters a condition defined by an alarm type that is being monitored by an Alarm agent. However, an

nd events to the necessary personnel and/or applications. In Adroit an incident occurs when an agent enters a condition defined by an alarm type that is being monitored by an Alarm agent. However, an incident is ONLY an alarm, if it needs to be responded to; otherwise it is an event. -->

About Alarm Types Top About Alarm Types An alarm type is simply the required condition or state of an agent that you need to alarm. This can also contain a list of slots of this agent, which are reported when the alarm occurs. In Adroit , each agent drives the following status bits: These status bits are divided into the following categories: Common Status Bits , which indicate their internal status (or integrity) and are common to all agents. For instance, these can indicate failures within the Adroit system itself. Specific Status Bits , which indicate the status of the values driven by or contained in the agent and are specific to each agent type. For instance, these can indicate plant upsets or process variable excursions. Each alarm type requires two of the following three components: specify which of these status bits must be simultaneously enabled or disabled and provide a descriptive name for the specified condition, this usually takes the form of a descriptive abbreviation. For instance "Overheating" for an Analog agent type or "Tripped" for a Digital agent type. if necessary, specify which slots of the agent should be reported when the specified condition occurs, in other

r instance "Overheating" for an Analog agent type or "Tripped" for a Digital agent type. if necessary, specify which slots of the agent should be reported when the specified condition occurs, in other words ONLY select those slots that will help clarify or troubleshoot this state of the agent. For instance: To create an alarm type : You can either create alarm types from the Alarm agent for ALL agent types or from the Alarming dialog for the agent type of the specific agent that you are alarming. To edit an alarm type :You can either edit alarm types from the Alarm agent for ALL agent types or from the Alarming dialog for the agent type of the specific agent that you are alarming. To remove an alarm type : You can ONLY remove alarm types from the Alarm agent for ALL agent types. When you ‘alarm’ an agent, you simply select the required alarm type/s that the specified Alarm agent should monitor for this agent. Then when the necessary status bit/s are set in this agent that match one of the selected Agent Types, the Alarm agent communicates incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Eac

the selected Agent Types, the Alarm agent communicates incidents signified by AgentName.AlarmType, which indicate that this agent has gone into the condition or state specified by this alarm type. Each incident can either be an alarm (requiring action) or an event (not requiring action). via the selected alarm route. Example: By default each agent type provides one or more pre-configured alarm types. This means that one set of alarm types will be created for Analog agents and another set for Digital agents. If necessary, you can create your own agent types. Although it is NOT recommended that you modify the predefined alarm types. Note: Alarm types are specified per agent type; therefore once you have created the required agent type for one agent it is available for ALL agents of this type. The default alarm types are pre-configured in the postload Adroit database file . For further details of this file, see About the Postload Database File . -->

text: About Backup Procedures Top About Backup Procedures It is important to create a backup procedure to guarantee disaster avoidance rather than just disaster recovery and also to provide an easy way for transferring an Adroit project or system to another computer. Hence, this backup procedure should include all the files utilised during plant operation and include storage facilities as well as locations, since critical data should be stored in an alternative location, such as a drive or remote hard disk etc. For these reasons it is recommended to use the System Backup and Restore facility provided by the Adroit Config Editor utility to execute and manage such a backup procedure. For details, see System Backup and Restore . Note: This requires you to have installed SmartUI . The backup process generates a single compressed file in the specified location, which contains the date and time of its creation, which contains all the relevant registry settings and all the files and folders containing the user-configuration of the currently specified Configuration. When restoring, you can restore between x86 and x64 operating system architectures and across different operating system language s

ing the user-configuration of the currently specified Configuration. When restoring, you can restore between x86 and x64 operating system architectures and across different operating system language sets. However, any file paths within the agent database (.wgp) file are not currently converted and still need to be manually edited after restoring the project. This backup includes the following files and settings: Adroit data files . This will backup up the files required by your Adroit projects, where multiple file locations can be specified. WGP files, provide two features to assist with their regular backup. For details, see Backing Up Adroit Database (.WGP) Files . WARNING! These features are merely intended to AUGMENT the existing backup system and NOT to REPLACE it i.e. it is still imperative that an efficient backup system is in place! Event Logs . This will ONLY export the application; security and system event logs files. These event log files CANNOT be restored but can be viewed by using the Event Viewer. Adroit registry. This will backup both the global Adroit registry settings and the Adroit registry settings specific to the current user. This will contain the Adroit conf

d by using the Event Viewer. Adroit registry. This will backup both the global Adroit registry settings and the Adroit registry settings specific to the current user. This will contain the Adroit configuration, workspaces and Adroit protocol driver configuration settings. -->

About Behaviors Top About Behaviours Behaviours can animate or provide additional functionality to controls and graphic elements (vectors) that you add to your graphic form. Click for more details: In other words you can typically use Behaviours to display the values of your data, either actually or graphically, by using the available properties of the selected control or graphic element and to perform other functions too. Available Behaviours The following Behaviours can be added to controls and/or graphic elements (vectors): Tip: You can use the Behaviours tab of the SmartUI Designer ribbon to add, edit or remove these Behaviours and in some cases the Child Behaviour option. For details, see Child Behaviours . Bind Value : to drive a data element (value) to and/or from the value of a property of a control or vector. Color : to assign colors to the two states of a digital (Boolean) value; to blink a specific color property or the VISIBILITY property either continuously or triggered by a value. You can also define states of color based on specific value ranges to provide a visual indication of a value. You can also define states of color based on a bit mask - a specific sequence of

a value. You can also define states of color based on specific value ranges to provide a visual indication of a value. You can also define states of color based on a bit mask - a specific sequence of bits that are set (to 1) for up to 32 bits to provide a visual indication of each bit mask. Display Value : to display and if necessary format a value. Execute Command : to perform commands, such as launching an application or opening, closing or printing a graphic form or logging a user on or off and/or switching users. Flip Bitmap : to create a defined sequence of images or a multi-image display, which can only be added to a Picture vector. Location : to dynamically move the object linearly in a defined X-Y direction by means of a monitored value. Operator Action : typically provides methods that allow end users to change a value at runtime. Percentage Fill : to dynamically fill the object by means of a monitored value. Rotation : to dynamically rotate the object by means of a monitored value. size : to dynamically resize the object linearly by means of a monitored value. Tooltip : to display additional information usually concerning this object when the mouse cursor (pointer) hover

value. size : to dynamically resize the object linearly by means of a monitored value. Each CSV Connector Link creates four CSV files that can be configured to provide the information necessary to configure a WGP file. Each of these files can create agents and are located in the CSV subfolder of the designated project folder, which is typically C:\ProgramData\Adroit Technologies\Adroit\Configurations\Default \CSV. Also queries now provide common tasks for managing your database, each with its own structured configuration dialog. Due to these improvements you can now use SmartUI as the generic front-end for all your databases to manage, view and configure their data. SmartUI connects to all the commonly used databases such as Access, Oracle or SQL Server, to name a few. In other words, SmartUI can expose the data (tables and fields) within any OLE DB The open standard for accessing data from a variety of sources. About DataBinders Top About DataBinders After connecting your database to an OLE DB datasource, you can add DataBinders to allow your users to view and/or modify the data within your database. Each DataBinder can create a sub-set of your data to select only the data that meets a specific need. In addition to selecting the required tables and their fields, you can also create relationships between the selected tables and/or add parameterised constraints and/or specify how the displayed data should be sorted. Typically relationships are only defined within the database program itself. This facility is provided to allow you to comprehensively configure your data by ONLY using SmartUI . For an example of using a DataBinder to read and/or write data in a database to and/from a control on a graphic form, see How to write and or read database data from a control . The main difference between a Select query and a DataBinder Although this seems similar to the function performed by a Select query, the main difference between a query and DataBinder is that: Select queries (and the queries in previous versions) only return static snapshots of the selected data that are only current at the time

y, the main difference between a query and DataBinder is that: Select queries (and the queries in previous versions) only return static snapshots of the selected data that are only current at the time at which the query is performed. DataBinders remain in constant communication with the database and so can provide a ‘live’ view of your data, if necessary. This makes it possible for DataBinders to modify the data within the database, so that instead of merely viewing the existing records, additional records can be added or existing records can be removed. About datasources and data elements Top About datasources and data elements The SmartUI Server is a "data portal" which integrates data from a number of disparate sources. Each source of data requires a datasource plugin before it can be associated with the SmartUI Server. This provides the ability to expose its data as data elements to the Server and, if necessary, provides special functions or methods to further interact with its data. Click for more details: For instance, the OLEDB datasource plugin exposes data within OLEDB databases to the Server as data elements. While the datasource plugin behaves as a datasource template, it is the datasource itself, which is the actual connection to each source of data wherever it is physically located. By using its datasource plugin, the datasource is able to expose the connected data to the Server as data elements. It also provides any special functions so that users can further interact with this connected data. For instance, an OLEDB datasource connects to an OLEDB database (e.g. Database1.mdb), by using the OLEDB datasource plugin to expose the tables and fields within this database as data elements to the Server. A data element is es

ource connects to an OLEDB database (e.g. Database1.mdb), by using the OLEDB datasource plugin to expose the tables and fields within this database as data elements to the Server. A data element is essentially a finite component of data contained within a datasource that behaves in a generic manner. In other words, although data elements may contain disparate data, they all possess generic attributes so that they can be similarly interacted and worked with. For instance, a data element would be a specific field within an OLEDB datasource e.g. Database1.mdb. Note1: In addition to making its data available as data elements, a datasource plugin may also or may only provide additional functionality for interacting with each datasource and/or its data, known as special functions. Note2: Each data element contains a number of internal properties, one of which monitors the status of the veracity or accuracy of its data. If this is set to anything other than GOOD, then any controls that displays this data element in a graphic form will become disabled (greyed out). For details on associating data elements with controls, see Animating graphic forms . Note3: Access to data elements and speci

ys this data element in a graphic form will become disabled (greyed out). For details on associating data elements with controls, see Animating graphic forms . Note3: Access to data elements and special functions need to be controlled separately for each datasource that is created. For details, see Working with data element security or Working with special function security . About Filtering Prioritised Incidents Top About Filtering Prioritised Incidents One way to ensure that your operators ONLY receive IMPORTANT alarms is to prioritise your alarms into categories of importance. Since some alarms are critical, whereas others are more informational in nature. Once you have prioritised your incidents, Adroit provides the following ways to filter your incidents, based on their priority: You can configure the priority level of each Alarm agent to discard any alarm that has a LOWER priority level. In this way you can to filter out the alarms of less important or less critical agents. WARNING! This method REMOVES the lower prioritised alarms so that they are NOT REPORTED. This method should ONLY be used during times of process upheaval or when alarm flooding occurs (this is indicative of a badly configured alarm configuration). To set the alarm priority filter of an Alarm Agent: Any incident that has a LOWER priority is DISCARDED by the Alarm agent and is as if this alarm did not exist at all. Edit the required Alarm agent. About Power Factor Top About Power Factor The importance of the power factor lies in the fact that electricity providers supply customers with volt-amperes, but bill them for watts. Power factors below 1.0 require an electricity provider to generate more than the minimum volt-amperes necessary to supply the real power (watts). Since this increases the electricity provider’s generation and transmission costs, they may charge additional costs to customers who have a power factor below some limit. In other words, most electric billing is done in kilowatt-hours, which is determined by the following equation: Kilowatt-hours = (Volts * Amperes) * power factor * run time If we assume that the run time, volts, and kilowatt-hours are constant, then as the power factor decreases the amperage must rise to compensate. The converse is also true, if the power factor is raised for a load, then the amperage is reduced. For this reason, by adjusting the power factor of a system to very near unity, you ONLY pay for the power that you use. A good power factor is considered to be greater than 0.85. To understand the power factor is more detail, it is necessary to know that the following three types of

ONLY pay for the power that you use. A good power factor is considered to be greater than 0.85. To understand the power factor is more detail, it is necessary to know that the following three types of power are used to describe energy flow in an alternating current (A.C.) electrical system: Real power is the actual power that is being used or the ability of the system to perform work and is measured in watts (kW). Apparent power is the power that the system seems to be using, being the product of the current and voltage of the circuit and is therefore measured in volt-amperes (kVA). Reactive power is ‘invisible’ or wattless power, in which energy stored in the load is returned to the source and is measured in kVAR, which stands for volt-amperes-reactive. The power factor of an alternating current (A.C.) electrical system is simply the ratio of the real power to the apparent power and is a number between 0 and 1. The following ‘power triangle’ describes the relationship between these three types of power: Therefore, from this power triangle the following can be seen: When there is no reactive power element, such as for a purely resistive load (i.e. heating elements, incandescent lig

ree types of power: Therefore, from this power triangle the following can be seen: When there is no reactive power element, such as for a purely resistive load (i.e. heating elements, incandescent lighting, etc.) then the actual and the apparent power are the same i.e. there is no reactive power and so the power factor is 1. When a reactive power element exists then the apparent power can be greater than the real power component, which decreases the power factor. This reactive power element can be generated by: Inductive loads such as transformers and motors (any type of wound coil) generate reactive power with current waveform lagging the voltage Capacitive loads such as capacitor banks or buried cable generate reactive power with current phase leading the voltage. It is often possible to adjust the power factor of a system to very near unity. This practice is known as power factor correction and is achieved by switching in or out banks of inductors or capacitors. For example the inductive effect of motor loads may be offset by locally connected capacitors and vice verse. About SNMP Top About SNMP The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is a trouble-free network management tool that can monitor and manage of diverse range of devices on a computer network, such as routers, switches, hubs, UPSs, printers, modems and computers. Any SNMP network management system requires the following components: A manager, which is responsible for managing and monitoring SNMP devices, by performing the required network management functions. Note: Any computer or terminal running a SNMP manager is known as a Network Management Station (the NMS). An agent (NOT to be confused with an Adroit Agent or tag-type), which is simply a piece of software running on a device that is required to be managed. This agent is responsible for retrieving and setting management data, known as managed objects, for its device. Note: Any device that does not have an agent is referred to as being unmanageable. These SNMP managed objects might be hardware, configuration parameters, performance statistics, and so on, that directly relate to the current operation of the device in question. For details, see SNMP Managed Objects . -->

About SNMP Traps About SNMP Traps SNMP traps are unsolicited SNMP messages that devices send to notify an SNMP manager of significant events. Each message is known as 'a trap of the event', hence the term SNMP traps. IMPORTANT: NEVER run the Windows SNMP Trap (listener) service because it conflicts with the Adroit SNMP trap functionality! Note: This agent does NOT require the Windows SNMP Service to function, this service is ONLY required on each computer that this agent monitors. Using SNMP traps can reduce the number of SNMP managed objects (values) that you need to monitor (poll) for each device. In other words, instead of monitoring every OID value on every device, by using SNMP traps, a device can simply inform its SNMPManager agent of the important values, which are then pushed to the SNMPManager when an event occurs. Note: This will also increase your required scan point allocation, since one scan point is consumed for every unique OID value that is polled, written to and/or trapped. To enable the receipt of traps for an SNMPManager agent: Check the Enable traps checkbox (BOOLEAN trapEnabled slot), in the Connection settings section of the Edit SNMP Manager Agent dialog, whi

pped. To enable the receipt of traps for an SNMPManager agent: Check the Enable traps checkbox (BOOLEAN trapEnabled slot), in the Connection settings section of the Edit SNMP Manager Agent dialog, which is cleared (disabled) by default. Note1: You also need to Enable polling (the start slot) before you will receive traps. Note2: Adroit relies on the SNMP Trap Service to receive traps, which is installed with the SNMP Service. By definition a trap can either be simple - one OID (unique or not) OR complex- multiple OIDs (unique or not). Click for how to handle traps: you need to create a script to process non-unique OIDs you can manually add unique OIDs to the OID list, so that the value of its associated Tag is updated when this trap is fired. The SNMP Manager provides the following two trap handling Queues (which are FIFO in nature i.e. First In, First Out): Note: The trap queues are processed from the oldest to the newest trap. the first or main trap queue collects all the incoming traps the second or work queue is used to hold the remainder variable sets (described below) for external parsing. This queue ensures that the trap handling scripts no longer need to ensure stack integr

aps the second or work queue is used to hold the remainder variable sets (described below) for external parsing. This queue ensures that the trap handling scripts no longer need to ensure stack integrity. So now the script ONLY needs to monitor the following two size slots to ensure correct operation: trapCount (INTEGER): The number of OIDs traps (and their sub-traps) contained in the main trap queue (for simple traps this is 1, for complex traps this is the number of OIDs [sub-traps] in this trap). trapWorkCount (INTEGER): The number of remainder OIDs sub traps contained in the working trap queue (for simple traps this is NOT used, for complex traps this is the number of remainder OIDs [sub-traps] in this trap, minus the first one which was passed through to the trap slots directly). One trap event may consist of one or more trap variable sets, and one trap variable set consists of the following set of slots: trapGeneric (INTEGER): An Integer value of the generic code or identification of this trap OID. trapSpecific (INTEGER): An Integer value of the specific code or identification of this trap OID. trapOID (VARSTRING): The OID, in numeric format, which identifies the SNMP managed

n of this trap OID. trapSpecific (INTEGER): An Integer value of the specific code or identification of this trap OID. trapOID (VARSTRING): The OID, in numeric format, which identifies the SNMP managed object for this event. trapValue (VARSTRING): The value of the OID specified by trapOID . trapTime (TIME): The time that the value, specified by trapValue , occurred. trapType (INTEGER): An Integer indicator of the return type of the value, specified by trapValue , for information purposes only. For details, see OID Return Type Indicators. This indicator can help you to determine which tag you should use to store this value. These slots are marked as empty when there is no trap to parse, so triggering trapPop is this case does nothing. ove for use by a domain specific script. trapPop (BOOLEAN): Set this slot to 1 (via a script or button etc.) to read the first trap off the main trap queue, which reduces the trapCount slot by the number of OIDs in this trap (for simple traps this is 1, for complex traps this is more than 1). The Adroit DB Generator creates Adroit agent databases (.WGP files) from information stored in 3 rd party applications, such as front-end devices. ult) Adroit groups and user can be created for you. The Windows Security Options branch: these settings apply to the Windows operating system. About the AlarmManagement Database Top About the AlarmManagement Database The OLE DB compatible database specified by an AlarmManagement agent is the repository of all the logged incidents. This database allows you to obtain reports and KPIs focused around delivering a clear set of information on which the operators can act. The AlarmManagement agent provides the View Data and View Graph dialogs to allow users to analyse the data contained in its database. However, we recommend that you install the Adroit Report Suite and specifically the Alarm Management Reports report pack , which provides you with the necessary tools you need to analyse and, more importantly, to improve your alarming system. For this reason, it is necessary to know the structure of the tables within the OLE DB database that the AlarmManagement agent populates. This database records all the incidents including the time of incident, time of acknowledgement and time the incident cleared. IMPORTANT: To clear the Alarm Management database - simply to delete all the tables and then restart the Agent Server, which recreates and populates the tables correctly. DO NOT use a script to empty this database, since many of th

anagement database - simply to delete all the tables and then restart the Agent Server, which recreates and populates the tables correctly. DO NOT use a script to empty this database, since many of the tables use an auto-incrementing index field, which is NOT reset in this case causing all manner of problems. WARNING! If you delete any of these tables, they will be recreated with their default configuration when the Agent Server is restarted, BUT you will LOSE any previous configuration or data that the tables may have contained. Each incident is logged using the name of its assigned AlarmManagement agent, so that it is possible to unify your alarm management for your enterprise and have more than one AlarmManagement agent log incidents to the SAME database. In this case please ensure that your AlarmManagement agent are uniquely named. The two primary tables in this database are the Adr_AM_CurrentIncidents and Adr_AM_HistoricalIncidents tables, which store all the logged incidents. An important field in these tables is the IncidentID field, which uniquely identifies each incident in this database. So by querying an entry in this field you can find out ALL the information pertaining

important field in these tables is the IncidentID field, which uniquely identifies each incident in this database. So by querying an entry in this field you can find out ALL the information pertaining to a specific alarm/event, such as every time this incident has been logged. ALL incidents found in the Adr_AM_CurrentIncidents table as a result of the last Agent Server session are marked as acknowledged and their active times are set to zero. If these entries do not require reasons and/or notes then they are automatically added to the Adr_AM_HistoricalIncidents table. If the entries require reasons and/or notes, then they will remain in the Adr_AM_CurrentIncidents table until these entries have been completed by the operator. For a description of each of the tables and their fields, see AlarmManagement Database Tables . -->

About the GSM_SMS driver Top About the GSM_SMS driver The sole function of the GSM_SMS driver is the sending and receiving of SMS messages to and from SMS GSM modems. This driver has been specifically designed to simply its use with any cellular SMS protocol. For this reason, Windows drivers for the modem are NOT required, since this driver provides its own interface to the modem via the serial port assigned to it. Note: This driver is ONLY designed to work with SMS GSM modems and, in particular, has been designed and tested using the WAVECOM WMOD2 GSM modem. The devices configured for this driver, can be used in one of following two modes, depending upon the configuration of its Use with Command Agent checkbox setting: Note: For details, concerning the configuration of devices, see Configuring Devices . If checked, the default setting, this device can only be used by a Command agent, which bypasses the scanning sub-system, so that the full SMS message of up to 160 characters can be utilised. In addition, the Command agent provides extensive functionality for both sending and receiving SMS messages. For further details, see Command Agents . If unchecked, this device uses the scanni

ilised. In addition, the Command agent provides extensive functionality for both sending and receiving SMS messages. For further details, see Command Agents . If unchecked, this device uses the scanning sub-system, as normal, replacing the former User-driver functionality, which was also difficult to configure, of sending 79 character SMS messages, configured in the Text, String or Notifier agents. Therefore the Notifier agent can still be used to automatically route alarms from Adroit by SMS to the relevant personnel. For details, see Notifier Agents . Note: The driver only handles the transmission of the intended message, which can originate as an alarm, a message entered by an operator or via programming performed in Adroit . -->

Accessing Agent Slots Top Accessing Agent Slots Because of Adroit ‘s open architecture, it is extremely easy to read and/or write agent slot values, provided you know the name of the agent and slot. For details, see About Agents or About Agent Data (Slots) . Slots within agents can be accessed, as follows: The actual agent itself may change values within one or more of its slots. An Expression agent, for example, will generate a new value whenever one of its inputs changes. Another agent within the same Agent Server may read or write one or more agents’ slots. For example, a Scan agent updates the agent(s) and slot(s) it scans whenever values in the front-end device change. Windows within the Adroit user interface can access slot values within agents. For example, Mimic Display Value Behaviours read slot values, whereas Mimic Operator Action Behaviours write slot values. Custom applications using the Agent Server Applications Programming Interface can access slot values. For instance OLE Interface or ActiveX Control . Note: All slots generally offer safe read access, but caution must be exercised when writing slot values. -->

Account Policy Top Account Policy The Windows based Account policy controls how passwords must be used by all user accounts. It defines such things as the maximum password age, minimum password age, minimum password length, and whether or not a password history is maintained. The Account policy determines whether all user accounts are subjected to lockout. If lockout is enabled, then a user account becomes locked if there are a number of incorrect attempts to log on to that account, occurring with no more than a specified amount of time between any two of the bad logon attempts. A locked account remains locked until an administrator unlocks it or a specified amount of time passes. Locked accounts cannot log on. The Account policy also determines whether or not a remote user will be forcibly disconnected from all connections to servers in the domain if that user’s logon hours expire, and whether users must log on before changing their passwords. -->

ACK Commands Top ACK Commands Function: To acknowledge alarms reported by an agent within the Agent Server. Note1: Alarms are always globally acknowledged. Note2: This command must be enabled by the Command agent , which it is sent to, before it can be performed, because it can create a security and operational risk through the remote acknowledgment of alarms. For details, see Specifying Permitted Commands . Note3: Both the command and its parameters are NOT case-sensitive; commands have only been capitalised for ease of reference. To globally acknowledge an alarm via SMS: ack,tag[.alarm type] Where ‘ tag ’ is the name of the agent a user wants to acknowledge, ‘[.alarm type]’ is optional and allows you to acknowledge a specific alarm for the specified agent. For instance “ANA_1.High” only acknowledges ANA_1.High, whereas “ANA_1” acknowledges ALL the alarms relating to the agent ANA_1. To acknowledge more than one alarm at a time, use the following format: ack,tag[.alarm type],…, tag[.alarm type] To globally acknowledge alarms via Putslot: use the new globalAck slot of the Command agent and use the following format: tag[.alarm type] Note: This method does NOT use SMS to acknowledge

larm type] To globally acknowledge alarms via Putslot: use the new globalAck slot of the Command agent and use the following format: tag[.alarm type] Note: This method does NOT use SMS to acknowledge alarms, nor are you limited to only using the Putslot utility, any method can be used that sets the value of this slot. Where ‘ tag ’ is the name of the agent a user wants to acknowledge, ‘[.alarm type]’ is optional and allows you to to acknowledge a specific alarm for the specified agent. To ensure that the Agent Server automatically acknowledges alarms at startup, either do NOT add this key or if you have added it, then set it to 1: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Adroit Technologies\Adroit\Workgroup\WG.INI (REG_)DWORD AcknowledgeAtStartup = 1, the default value is 1. AcknowledgeAtStartup Top Active Link Monitoring WARNING: Registry settings are recorded as ADVANCED information and should not be used unless you understand exactly how these will affect the operation of your Adroit installation, IF YOU HAVE ANY DOUBTS, PLEASE CONTACT Adroit SUPPORT, BEFORE CHANGING THE REGISTRY. PLEASE NOTE: When working on a 64 bit operating system, remember to add "\Wow6432Node" to the path of each registry setting after "\SOFTWARE", for instance: "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Adroit Technologies". The following Active Link Monitoring registry settings can remedy or troubleshoot slow (or unresponsive) Agent Servers and/or clients, which may occur when: there are a large number of clients connected to an Agent Server AND/OR there is a misbehaving network and/or clients resulting in an inability to effectively send subscriptions to the Agent Server. These (REG_)DWORD registry settings need to be added to the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Adroit Technologies\Adroit\Workgroup\WG.INI registry key: ActiveLinkMonitor : when set to a value of 1, this enables an Agent Server’s link manager to actively monitor connections to remote Agent Servers instead of simply

droit\Workgroup\WG.INI registry key: ActiveLinkMonitor : when set to a value of 1, this enables an Agent Server’s link manager to actively monitor connections to remote Agent Servers instead of simply relying on broadcasts from the remote Agent Server to assume that the connection is healthy. This setting works hand in hand with the KillSlowClients registry setting, for instance, if the remote Agent Server has KillSlowClients enabled, then the remote Agent Server will force a disconnection to the local (this) Agent Server should the remote Agent Server be unable to send subscriptions to the local (this) Agent Server. The ActiveLinkMonitor setting allows the local Agent Server to recognise this closed channel within 5 seconds - instead of the legacy 30 to 45 seconds that potentially causes secondary issues with the local Agent Server and any clients connected to it. Active Clusters Foundation Top Clustering Agent Servers Clustered Agent Servers, previously known as hot standby, provide both client and server redundancy enabling high availability of the system. Typically, redundancy can be applied to all the levels within the plant. For more details on addressing the important issues that affect the operation and configuration of clustered Adroit Agent Servers, see Important Points to consider when Clustering Agent Servers . There are three general components in Adroit which are aware of redundancy, namely, the clients, the servers and the server I/O, as illustrated below: In Adroit , an Agent Server can be setup to be a cluster server, which is a set of two Agent Servers running a replicated database (WGP file) on the same project. A cluster Agent Server can be networked with other normal (non-cluster) Agent Servers. The general idea of clustering is that the master server services all the I/O and client tasks, while the standby server replicates the master server. If the master server or computer fails, the standby server takes over as master and the UI’s and scanning tasks take appropriate action. There are three key mechanisms in Active Clu

the master server. If the master server or computer fails, the standby server takes over as master and the UI’s and scanning tasks take appropriate action. There are three key mechanisms in Active Clusters namely catch-up , replication and switchover . A clustered Agent Server: can be networked with other normal (non-cluster) Agent Servers. is either in the mode of master or standby server is either in the state of healthy or unhealthy. A cluster Agent Server is either in the mode of master or standby server and can either be in the state of healthy or unhealthy. Note: Certain agent types on a cluster server require synchronization of internal data structures with their master partner. For details, see Real-time Catch-up . Also, some agents in an Agent Server have internal states that are unknown to and unsynchronised with the standby computer. Examples of such agents are: the Expression agent, the Recipe agent, the Counter agent, the Statistical agent and all other internal agents that do some calculation internal to the Agent Server. All cluster information and operations including the historical synchronization can be viewed and managed within the UI by using the cluster-control

See the Active Cluster Control tab of the System Management graphic form in the System Information project. Add a Group Top Add a Group Tag groups are primarily added to manage the communication settings for the tags whose values need to be communicated to or from the remote Agent Servers via their associated WanServers. Groups are server-specific. For details, see Tag Groups . To add a group: If necessary launch the WanClient and open the WanClient Configurator, by selecting the Open Configurator item from the File menu. Ensure that the required server is selected in the Select server list box. For details, see Servers . Click the Add Group button to display the Create New Group dialog. In the Group Title edit box, specify a name for this tag group, which must not be more than 90 characters in length. In the Group Type list box, select the communication type required by the tag links within the group, from the following options: Normal: This should contain tag links, whose local values (located in the Agent Server, residing on the WanClient computer) should ONLY be fetched (read) from the specified remote tag values via the required WanServers. Control: This should contain tag links, whose local values (located in the Agent Server, residing on the WanClient computer) can be BOTH fetched

pecified remote tag values via the required WanServers. Control: This should contain tag links, whose local values (located in the Agent Server, residing on the WanClient computer) can be BOTH fetched (read) from AND sent (written) to the specified remote tag values via the required WanServers. In the Poll Period edit box, specify the rate in seconds at which the WanClient should request this WanServer for changes to the tag links within this tag group. The default value of 0 implies "as fast as possible" and specifies a 1 second polling rate. Note: Poll periods can be specified from 1 to 2000 seconds. Click the Ok button to add the group or the Cancel button to discard the settings and return to the WanClient Configurator. Note: If the OK button is clicked, without all the fields being completed, a message box appears requesting that all the fields are completed first. -->

Add a Link Top Add a Link A tag link or tag mapping, specifies the name of the local and the remote Adroit tag, whose values are to be ‘linked’. This is added to a tag group within a server. For details, see Tag Links . To add a link: If necessary launch the WanClient and open the WanClient Configurator, by selecting the Open Configurator item from the File menu. Ensure that the required server is selected in the Select server list box. For details, see Servers . Ensure that the required tag group is selected in the Select group list box. For details, see Tag Groups . Click the New Link button to display the New Link dialog. In the Remote Tag edit box, specify the name of the required Adroit tag (agent.slot), located in the Agent Server residing on the WanServer computer. In the Local Tag edit box, specify the name of the required Adroit tag (agent.slot), located in the local Agent Server, residing on the WanClient computer. The Method list box, is disabled, since this only applies to tags within normal groups, in which case the WanServer will return the current value of the specified remote tag. Add a Server Top Add a Server A Server simply stores the necessary communication settings for a specific remote WanServer and its computer, so that the WanClient can connect to this computer and communicate with this WanServer application. For further details, see Servers . To add a server: If necessary launch the WanClient and open the WanClient Configurator, by selecting the Open Configurator item from the File menu. Click the Add Server button to display the New Remote Server dialog. In the Full server title edit box, specify a name for the server, not more than 90 characters in length. In the Database name edit box, specify the name to be used by this server to store its tag groups and tag links. This will be saved as a CSV file in the database folder , which is created in the folder in which WanClient has been installed. Tip: This file can also be edited manually for bulk configuration of tag groups and bulk configuration of tag links . Note: This filename should be not more than 90 characters in length.
